subject: How to change adjustments in log regression models (-->Design)?

messages.author: eb09e8497b635c23
messages.subject: How to change adjustments in log regression models (-->Design)?
parts:
hi guys,

"plot.Design" offers some neat ways of plotting the effects of one or
two predictors of a (logistic) regression model.
By default, all non-plotted variables are set to their respective
reference levels

My question is: Does anybody know if/how these reference levels can be
changed/re-defined?

From the help file ( http://127.0.0.1:15668/library/Design/html/plot.Design.html
) I have learned that it is possible to adjust all non-plotted
variables to 0 (or reference cell for categorical variables) by
setting "adj.zero" to TRUE. Now, while this gives me some confidence
in assuming that one can play around with the adjustments, that's not
quite what I want (as this also instructs R to omit intercept(s) from
consideration, which I find confusing). Ideally, I would like to
change the reference value of just ONE selected variable.

Any ideas? (besides relabelling the original data such that the
"correct" reference level will be chosen by default)

Thanks!

--Daniel

Not that that's elegant or anything - because it's not - but as a
quick and dirty fix to get, can't you just

- change the reference level before you do the data.dist and then the
lrm? or, more generally
- write a wrapper function that uses relevel to change the reference
level to what you want, run data.dist and the lrm again (with
lrm(formula(previous.model)), and plots it?

messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] How to change adjustments in log regression models (-->Design)?
parts:
Two quick follow-up questions:

(i) You wrote: "By default, all non-plotted variables are set to their
respective reference levels" - well, not on my machine. On my machine,
the level chosen for adjustment is not the reference level (i.e., the
alphabetically first) but the most frequent one.

(ii) You have made sure that the default plot dooesn't get distorted
by an interaction? When I apply

par(mfrow=c(1,2)); plot(model.01, fun=plogis)

to the data/model discussed in Section 2.4 of this paper
<http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/research/XXX_STG-SW_RegrTransl_XXX.pdf>,
then I get the slope adjusted for weil/because, which are so *not*
indicative of what happens in this data set, as you can see on p. 11
of the same paper.

Just checking ...

STG

messages.author: cd4fa709cb39cadc

parts:
Hi Stefan,

thanks for your comments!

@ (i) : oh yes, sorry, you are right; of course, the adjusted values are the most frequent ones...(but the question still remains)

@ (ii) : hm...I am not quite sure I understand what you mean by the plot "getting distorted" but the reason for why I would like to change the reference level in the effect plot has indeed a lot to do with interactions.

Figure 2 in your example can certainly help to illustrate my problem: we observe that LengthDiff has different effects for each conjunction (=> interaction LengthDiff & CONJ). As long as the model comprises only these two variables (and their interaction), we get all the info we need from a plot like the one in Figure 2, right? (One would say something like: plot(model.01, LengthDiff=NA, CONJ=NA, fun=plogis, ...) # right?)

But let's suppose there are additional factors in the model. I understand that plot.Design only permits a maximum of 2 variables to NOT get adjusted. If I now wanted to see the effect for LengthDiff AND some other variable VARx, I would specify LengthDiff and VARx as "NA" in plot.Design. The variable CONJ would then be set to the most frequent level/conjunction, which then may result in a plot that does not really give us an adequate picture of what is going on. That is to say, if there are interactions among the variables, the plot captures only a part of what is going on.In my case, the adjustment of one of the not depicted variables happens to be set to the most atypical scenario (not unlike "before" in your example (--> the other two, "nachdem" & "als" show different signs, so in a way adjusting CONV to "before" would portray an 'atypical scenario' (leaving "weil" aside for the moment)). Is that what you were alluding to?

@ can't you just change the reference level before you do the data.dist and then the lrm? :
use relevel(), eh? hm, I guess I could do that. But that's similar to re-labelling the original input data with a numeric prefix or something but it would produce a whole new model summary, right? On the other hand, it may be the better work-around as it would not result in odd labels of factor levels in the plots.

I am definitely gonna play around with that. Thanks!
But I still can't believe that there must be a better way - especially since "adj.zero" shows the reference levels can be changed at the time plot is produced.

Thanks again,
cheers,
Daniel

ok, just checking, coulda been a change in the package or something

> @ (ii) : hm...I am not quite sure I understand what you mean by the plot "getting distorted" but the reason for why I would like to change the reference level in the effect plot has indeed a lot to do with interactions.

I mean that sometimes the most frequent level doesn't really capture
best at what's going on in the data. Like in the Figure 2 example,
where choosing any conjunction would give a very bad overview of what
the other levels are doing, and I think that's what you described in
the then following paragraph of your mail (interestingly, the p-value
for the interaction is not even super-low although the effects are
quite strong in the graph).

>> can't you just change the reference level before you do the data.dist and then the lrm? :
> use relevel(), eh? hm, I guess I could do that. But that's similar to re-labelling the original input data with a numeric prefix or something but it would produce a whole new model summary, right?

it would, yes, but without the annoying numbering, which might show up
in the graph when functions pick the factor levels automatically, as
you yourself mention
> But I still can't believe that there must be a better way - especially since "adj.zero" shows the reference levels can be changed at the time plot is produced.

Yes, there may well be. You probably know plot.Design better than me
already because I never use it: I prefer to put together my graph from
the very start, but I admit that may be very old-fashioned - the
advantage is, you're in the driver's seat and not dependent on a
particular implementation. In a way, it's why one does R and not SPSS
on the micro-level of plotting: being able to tweak everything; I
think something like Figure 2 is a very good representation but I
don't think it's possible with Design (with ggplot2 tho it would be
not that hard, have you tried that - generating a data frame of
predictions and then using qplot?) . But enough of the proselytizing,
and I understand that sometimes one may be reluctant to do it all by
hand ;-) Maybe someone else can help more with plot.Design than me ...

Cheers,
